slots.mapDescription: Caddy, Anubis, the Rails web app, the Solid Queue worker and four SQLite databases, with the paths a page view, a vote, a comment and a new story take.
slots.completionLessons:
• Why most visitors never reach Rails: Caddy serves cached HTML files
  • How one vote becomes a new score and hotness in a single UPDATE
  • How a comment turns into a reply email and a push, after the response
  • Why one server with SQLite and a database-backed queue is enough
slots.completionIntro: You followed a page view through the full-page cache, a vote into the ranking, a comment out to an inbox and a new story out to the web.

panels.introHtml:
Start here

Lobsters, the link aggregator

A map of lobsters/lobsters in C4 terms: context on the overview, the web server, the Rails app, its background worker and its databases on the full map.

Lobsters was created by joshua stein and is developed by its contributors; it is released under the 3-clause BSD licence. This map describes it in its own words and is not affiliated with its authors.

Try it

  • Open a card to see its part of the system.
  • Play A visitor opens the front page: most requests end at a file on disk.
  • Click a component for what it does and where it lives in the code.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

One server, one Rails app, four SQLite files

Production runs on a single VPS set up with Hatchbox: Caddy in front, Anubis as a bot filter, Puma running Rails, and a Solid Queue process for background jobs. Data lives in four SQLite databases; the queue and the cache are databases too.

How to read it

People on the left, the front door next, then the Rails app, the worker and the stores. Logged-out page views are mostly answered by Caddy from public/cache/; Rails refills those files after every write.

people.title: Readers and members
people.text: Logged-out visitors and feed readers, invited members who submit, vote and comment, and moderators with their own tools.

front.title: Front door
front.line2: and a mail server on the host.
front.text: Caddy terminates TLS and serves cached pages; Anubis challenges bots before Rails; Postfix sends mail and passes replies back in.

pages.title: Read pages
pages.text: The front page, /newest, tag and domain pages, feeds and search; logged-out views are written to disk and served by Caddy next time.

write.title: Post, vote, moderate
write.text: Submitting stories, commenting (on the site or by email), voting and flagging, and the moderation tools. The models recompute score and hotness on every vote.

background.title: Background work
background.text: Notifications, link previews and webmentions run as jobs; recurring tasks and two cron scripts keep caches, stats, backups and the Mastodon bot going.

storage.title: Storage
storage.text: The primary database holds everything users create; Solid Cache and Rack::Attack use their own files; Solid Queue keeps its jobs in a fourth.

outside.title: Outside services
outside.text: The web pages stories link to, the Mastodon instance the bot posts to, and Pushover for phone notifications.

nodes.what: Someone reading without logging in: a browser, an RSS reader or a crawler. Gets the same HTML as every other visitor.
nodes.why: Most traffic is logged out, so the whole caching design is built around this reader: no session cookie, no per-user HTML, no JavaScript.

nodes.what: A logged-in user, admitted by invitation unless signups are opened. Submits stories, comments, votes and flags, filters tags, and in mailing-list mode can reply by email.
nodes.why: Every write comes from a member. A logged-in request carries a session cookie, which makes Caddy skip the cached file and go to Rails.

nodes.what: A member with is_moderator: edits, deletes and merges stories, bans domains and users, reads mod mail and the flag and hotspot dashboards.
nodes.why: The site is run by volunteers, so moderation is built into the app rather than an admin console; every action is logged publicly in /moderations.

nodes.what: Terminates TLS, redirects to HTTPS, blocks some bots, and for a request without an app cookie serves the page straight from public/cache/. It also answers /c/<short_id> with a 302 from a redirect file that Rails wrote under shared/comment_redirects/c. Anything else goes on to Anubis on port 9000.
nodes.why: This is the reason a small server copes: a cached front page is a static file and never wakes Ruby.

nodes.what: A proof-of-work challenge proxy listening on 127.0.0.1:9000 and forwarding to Puma on 9001, with its own bot policy file.
nodes.why: Scrapers that hammer uncached pages would otherwise land on Rails. The app keeps Anubis's cookie and Caddy ignores it when deciding whether to serve a cached file.

nodes.what: Runs on the same server, set up from hatchbox/. Sends the app's mail on port 25, relayed through a hosted SMTP service and signed with DKIM. Mail to the site's domain is piped to script/lobsters-ingress, which posts it to Action Mailbox.
nodes.why: Reply notifications and password resets need mail; replies to mailing-list emails come back in as comments.

nodes.what: Rack::Attack throttles each IP, config/routes.rb picks the controller, and ApplicationController loads the user from session[:u] (set to the user's session_token by LoginController at login), drops unknown cookies, and clears the session cookie for anonymous visitors.
nodes.why: Clearing the cookie is what keeps logged-out visitors on the cached path: Caddy only serves a file when there is no app cookie.

nodes.what: The front page, /newest, /active, /top, tag, category, domain and origin pages, as HTML, JSON or RSS. Lists come from Story scopes, 25 per page.
nodes.why: These are the most-read pages. For anonymous visitors each list is cached for 45 seconds and the rendered page is written to disk with caches_page.

nodes.what: Parses a query with tag:, domain:, submitter:, title: and quoted terms, then matches story text or comments through SQLite FTS5 tables.
nodes.why: Search runs in the main database with no search server, in line with the project's rule of few moving parts.

nodes.what: After a vote, comment or edit, Rails enqueues CachePageJob for the story's page. The job renders the path in-process as an anonymous request and writes the HTML file. PrefillPageCacheJob warms the busiest pages every 2 minutes; RefillStoryPageCacheJob rewrites every story page after a deploy.
nodes.why: Pages are refreshed by a job instead of being deleted, so Caddy keeps serving a file and no visitor waits for a render.

nodes.what: Rendered HTML, JSON and RSS files named after their URL, shared between deploys. A cron job deletes files older than 3 minutes, except story pages under s/, which jobs rewrite.
nodes.why: A file on disk that Caddy can serve is the cheapest possible response. The writer is patched to write atomically so Caddy never serves a half-written file.

nodes.what: Submit, edit, delete, upvote, flag, hide and save stories. A new URL is fetched to suggest a title; a saved story enqueues a link preview job and, five minutes later, a webmention.
nodes.why: Every action that changes a story ends by asking for its cached page to be rebuilt, in one after_action.

nodes.what: Post, edit, delete, vote and flag comments, plus the comments feed and threads pages. A posted comment enqueues NotifyCommentJob.
nodes.why: Replies are the core of the site. The controller answers at once; notifying people happens in the worker.

nodes.what: Vote.vote_thusly_on_story_or_comment_for_user_because records a vote, adjusts karma and has the story or comment recount its score from the votes table. Stories then get a new hotness, comments a new confidence.
nodes.why: Ranking lives in the models, so every entry point shares it. Site votes and flags end in the update_score_and_recalculate! recount, and so does a comment's own upvote, which Comment#record_initial_upvote creates directly. A new story's own upvote skips the recount and karma (update_counters is false); its first hotness is set in assign_initial_attributes.

nodes.what: InboxMailbox takes mail addressed to <shortname>-<token>@, finds the member by mailing-list token and the parent from In-Reply-To, strips signatures and quotes, and saves a comment.
nodes.why: Members in mailing-list mode get new stories and comments by email (from script/mail_new_activity.rb, whose Reply-To is that address) and can answer from their mail client. That script is commented out in script/lobsters-cron, so this path probably sees little use today. Anything it cannot match is bounced.

nodes.what: Dashboards of flagged stories and comments, the hotspot list of comments scored by a naive Bayes model, mod notes, mod mail, domain and origin bans, story merges and tag edits. Moderator actions are recorded as Moderation rows, shown publicly at /moderations.
nodes.why: Flags only hide content from the ranking; people decide. The tools put the evidence in one place and the log keeps moderators accountable.

nodes.what: For each new comment: notify the story's submitter (if following) and the parent comment's author, then anyone @-mentioned. Each gets one Notification row, and by their settings an email and a Pushover push.
nodes.why: Emailing inside the request would make posting slow and fragile; as a job, a failed send never loses the comment.
nodes.tools: app/jobs/notify_comment_job.rb · app/mailers/email_reply_mailer.rb · extras/pushover.rb · sibling jobs notify_message_job.rb and notify_mod_mail_message_job.rb do the same for private messages and mod mail

nodes.what: Fetch the linked page's card image and save a PNG under public/story_image/; five minutes after submission, look for a webmention endpoint on the page and notify it.
nodes.why: Both talk to arbitrary sites, so they run out of the request with timeouts, through Sponge, which refuses private IP addresses.

nodes.what: Scheduled in config/recurring.yml: prefill the page cache every 2 minutes, WAL checkpoint every minute, traffic stats every 5 minutes, flagged commenters every 15, hotspot refresh hourly, stats graphs, sitemap and a Restic backup nightly. A few also fetch outside lists: a disposable-email blocklist weekly, the IANA TLD list monthly.
nodes.why: The queue's own scheduler replaces most cron entries, so jobs share one process, one log and the Mission Control dashboard.

nodes.what: Two crontab entries: script/expire_page_cache every minute and script/lobsters-cron every 5 minutes, which runs script/mastodon_post.rb to post up to ten hot stories that have not been posted yet.
nodes.why: These predate Solid Queue. The mailing-list script is still in the repo but commented out in lobsters-cron.

nodes.what: Users, stories, comments, votes, tags, notifications, messages, moderation logs, plus FTS5 tables for search. Backed up nightly: ResticJob copies it with .backup and pushes it, with logs and config, to a restic repository whose location is set in shared/etc/restic-env, outside the repo.
nodes.why: One file on the same disk: no database server to run. The app builds its own SQLite with compile flags, so the README says to use bin/sqlite3.

nodes.what: Two Solid Cache shards in their own files: cache.sqlite3 for Rails.cache (story lists, RSS, debounce keys) and rack_attack.sqlite3 for the rate limiter's counters.
nodes.why: Throttle counters churn constantly; giving them their own file keeps them from evicting useful cache entries.

nodes.what: Jobs, ready and scheduled executions, recurring tasks and concurrency semaphores. Two queues matter: default and refill_story_pages, which only one worker serves.
nodes.why: A queue in a database means no Redis. Semaphores give limits_concurrency, so the same page is never rendered twice at once.

nodes.what: The pages stories point to. Lobsters fetches them to suggest a title, find a card image and send a webmention.
nodes.why: Fetching user-supplied URLs is risky, so every request goes through Sponge with short timeouts and a block on private networks.

nodes.what: The bot account posts hot stories (score 2 or more, under two days old, not tagged meta) that have not been posted yet; members can also link their own Mastodon account in settings.
nodes.why: Followers on the fediverse see stories without visiting the site.

nodes.what: A push notification service. Members who connect it get replies and mentions on their phone.
nodes.why: An alternative to email for people who want to answer quickly; it is skipped entirely when no API token is configured.

frontpage.title: A visitor opens the front page
frontpage.desc: A logged-out reader asks for /. Most of the time Caddy answers from a file; on a miss Rails renders the page and writes the file for the next reader.

hops.t: The browser sends GET / with no app cookie. Caddy's cookie map treats an Anubis-only cookie as no cookie, and there is no ?token=.
Caddy tries public/cache/index.html. On a hit it rewrites the request to that file, adds a CSP header and is done: Rails never sees the request.
On a miss (expired by cron, or never written) the request goes to Anubis on port 9000, which may ask the browser to solve a challenge first.
Anubis forwards to Puma on 9001. Rack::Attack applies its per-IP throttles, the router picks home#index, and no user is loaded because there is no session.
HomeController#index asks for the hottest stories, page 1.
For anonymous visitors the story list is read through Rails.cache with a 45-second lifetime, so most renders skip the query.
On a cache miss Story.hottest runs: visible, unmerged, not hidden, non-negative score, ordered by the stored hotness column, 26 rows to know whether there is a next page.
caches_page fires because there is no user, no tag-filter cookie and an empty session, and writes the HTML to public/cache/index.html for the next visitor.

upvote.title: A member upvotes a story
upvote.desc: One click recounts the story's score and hotness in a single UPDATE, then a job re-renders the story's cached page.

hops.t: The click sends POST /stories/<short_id>/upvote with the session cookie, so Caddy does not look for a cached file.
Caddy proxies to Anubis; the member already holds its cookie.
Rails loads the user from session[:u]. Without one, the action answers 400 instead of redirecting, since it is called from JavaScript.
StoriesController#upvote refuses deleted or merged stories, then calls the vote method with +1.
Vote.vote_thusly… finds or starts this member's vote row, works out the score and flag change, and saves the vote. The submitter gains one karma unless they voted for themselves.
One UPDATE recounts score and flags from the votes table (ignoring flags from people who commented) and stores the new hotness computed from score, comments, tags and age.
The controller's after_action calls refill_story_page_cache: a 2-minute debounce key in the cache, then a CachePageJob for the story's path. The response is just ok.
A worker thread claims the job. limits_concurrency discards a second job for the same path while one runs.
The job renders the story page through the app in-process, as an anonymous HTTPS request, exactly as a visitor would see it.
The HTML is written atomically over public/cache/s/<short_id>/<slug>.html, and files with older title slugs are removed. The next visitor gets the new score from Caddy.

comment.title: A comment reaches the person it answers
comment.desc: A member replies to a comment. The request saves it and returns; the worker writes the notification and sends an email and a push.

hops.t: The reply form posts to /comments with the story's short id and the parent comment's short id.
Logged in, so straight past the page cache to Anubis.
The session gives @user; the router picks comments#create.
The controller checks the story still exists, the parent belongs to it, the text is not a double submit and the member is not over the speed limit.

Saving the comment sets its thread and depth; after commit it records the author's own upvote, recomputes the comment's confidence and the story's comment count and hotness, and queues a hotspot index job.
The comment row, its FTS5 entry and the vote are written; the story gets last_comment_at, the parent last_reply_at.
NotifyCommentJob.perform_later goes on the queue and the browser gets the rendered comment back. A page refill for the story is queued too.
The worker picks the job up and finds who should hear: the parent's author if active, and the submitter if following the story. People who hid the story are skipped.
One Notification row per person; a unique index means nobody is notified twice for the same comment.
If the recipient wants reply emails, EmailReplyMailer.reply goes out over SMTP to the local Postfix. A send error is swallowed.
Postfix relays the DKIM-signed mail. Its Message-Id, In-Reply-To and References headers thread it with the story's other emails in the member's mail client.
If the recipient enabled Pushover replies, the same text is pushed to their phone through Pushover's API.
The member sees the reply on their phone with a link straight to it.

submit.title: A member submits a story
submit.desc: While the form is filled in, the URL is fetched to suggest a title. Posting the form saves the story with its first vote and hotness, and two jobs reach back out to the linked site.

hops.t: The member opens /stories/new and pastes a URL; the page's script calls /stories/fetch_url_attributes (or the member arrives at /stories/new?url= from the bookmarklet).
Logged in, so the request goes through Anubis to Rails.
require_logged_in_user and, for new, verify_user_can_submit_stories run before the action.
StoriesController#fetch_url_attributes (or #new) builds a throwaway story from the URL.
Rails fetches the page with Sponge (3-second timeout, private IPs refused) to suggest its title and canonical URL; PDFs are read too. The title lands in the form, which the member can edit.
The member posts the form to /stories. StoriesController#create builds the story from the form; it does not fetch the URL again.
Validation checks tags, duplicates, banned domains and origins, and new-user rules. On create the story gets a short id, its submitter's upvote and its first hotness.
The story, its taggings and the vote are saved in one transaction; links in the text are recorded.
CreateStoryCardJob is queued now, SendWebmentionJob with a 5-minute wait, and the member is redirected to the new story.
The worker runs the card job: one job per story at a time.
It reads the page's card image and saves a PNG; minutes later the webmention job finds the site's endpoint, if any, and posts the story's URL to it.

emailreply.title: A mailing-list member replies by email
emailreply.desc: Answering a mailing-list email posts a comment, through Postfix and Action Mailbox. The script that sends those emails is currently disabled in cron.

hops.t: Mailing-list emails carry Reply-To: <shortname>-<mailing list token>@ the site's domain, so the member's reply goes there.
Postfix pipes it to script/lobsters-ingress, which posts it to /rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails with the ingress password. A failure exits 75 so Postfix retries.

InboxMailbox finds the member by token and the parent comment or story from In-Reply-To, takes the plain-text part, strips the signature and quoted text, and saves a comment marked is_from_email. Anything unmatched bounces.
The comment's own callbacks record its first vote and update the story's counts, as for a comment posted on the site.

buildSteps.title: A list of links
buildSteps.text: A Rails app on SQLite with stories, a front page ordered by hotness, and Caddy in front.
buildSteps.decision: Hotness is stored on the row and recomputed on writes, so the front page is an ORDER BY on an index.

buildSteps.title: Members and votes
buildSteps.text: Logins, story submission, and votes that move a story's score and hotness.
buildSteps.decision: Score and flags are recounted from the votes table in one UPDATE instead of incremented.

buildSteps.title: Serve pages from disk
buildSteps.text: Write anonymous pages to files that Caddy serves, and a job queue that rebuilds them after every change.
buildSteps.decision: Refill the file with a job instead of deleting it, so a visitor never waits for a render.

buildSteps.title: Comments and notifications
buildSteps.text: Threaded comments, and a job that tells the people being answered.
buildSteps.decision: Notify in the worker so posting stays fast and a failed email loses nothing.

buildSteps.title: Search, previews and caching
buildSteps.text: FTS5 search, link previews and webmentions, and a cache database for lists and throttling.
buildSteps.decision: Stay inside SQLite: full-text search, cache and rate-limit counters are all tables.

buildSteps.title: Keep it civil
buildSteps.text: Moderation tools and a bot filter in front of Rails.
buildSteps.decision: Moderators act in the app and every action is logged in public.

buildSteps.title: Mail in and out
buildSteps.text: Postfix on the host sends mail and turns replies into comments.
buildSteps.decision: Run the mail server on the same box rather than depend on a mail API.

buildSteps.title: Reach the fediverse
buildSteps.text: Cron scripts that post front-page stories to Mastodon and sweep the page cache.
buildSteps.decision: Leave the old cron scripts alone while new schedules go in recurring.yml.

tour.title: A community site on one server
body: Lobsters is a link aggregator: members submit links, vote and discuss them in threads, and moderators keep it on topic.
It runs as one Rails app on one VPS, with SQLite for data, cache and queue, and Caddy in front.
tour.why: The README is explicit: few moving parts, almost no external services, self-hosted from the VPS up. Everything on this map follows from that.

tour.title: Most reads are files
body: A logged-out visitor with no app cookie gets a page Caddy reads from disk.
tour.why: Rails is never involved in a cache hit, which is how a small server handles a busy site.

tour.title: A miss renders and writes the file
body: On a miss the request goes through Anubis to Rails, the story list comes from a 45-second cache or the database, and the rendered page is written to disk.
tour.why: Rails clears the session cookie for anonymous visitors so their next request stays on the cached path.

tour.title: A vote recounts the story
body: The vote row is saved, karma moves, and one SQL statement recounts score and flags and stores the new hotness.
tour.why: Recounting from the votes table instead of adding one keeps the score correct even when a flag stops counting because its author commented.

tour.title: Then the page is rebuilt
body: A job renders the story page as an anonymous visitor would see it and writes the file Caddy serves.
tour.why: The old file stays in place until the new one is ready, so nobody ever waits for a render.

tour.title: Submitting a story
body: The URL is fetched for a title while the form is filled in, the story is saved on submit with its first vote and hotness, and two jobs reach back out to the site.
tour.why: Every fetch of a user-supplied URL goes through Sponge, which refuses private IP addresses.

tour.title: A reply finds its reader
body: The comment is saved in the request; the worker writes notifications and sends email and pushes.
tour.why: The request returns as soon as the comment is saved; mail and push failures happen in the worker, out of the member's way.

tour.title: Replying by email
body: Postfix hands a reply to a mailing-list email to Action Mailbox, which saves it as a comment.
tour.why: The reply's In-Reply-To header names the comment or story it answers; the address's token names the member. Note that the mailing-list sender is commented out in cron.

tour.title: The whole site, on one map

recap.people: Visitors read, members post and vote, moderators keep order.
recap.front: Caddy serves cached pages, Anubis filters bots, Postfix handles mail.
recap.pages: Story lists and search, written to disk for logged-out readers.
recap.write: Stories, comments and votes; the models keep score and hotness.
recap.background: Solid Queue jobs and cron: notify, refill, preview, post.
recap.storage: Four SQLite files: data, cache, throttle counters and queue.
recap.outside: Linked sites, Mastodon and Pushover, all over HTTPS.

body: One Rails codebase run as a web server and a job worker, sharing SQLite files on one disk.
The idea that shapes it: logged-out pages are files, and every write ends by rebuilding the file it changed.

ranking.title: Inside a vote
ranking.sub: What Vote.vote_thusly_on_story_or_comment_for_user_because does with one click, then how the story recounts itself.
ranking.cap: The score is not incremented: it is recounted from the votes table in the same UPDATE that stores the new hotness. Flags from members who commented on the story are left out of both score and flag count.

steps.d: One row per member per story (or comment).
Avoids a rare deadlock with a story being created at the same moment.
Score moves only on upvotes; flags move only on flags.
Not when voting on your own story.
One UPDATE with subqueries over votes, plus the new hotness.
Tag modifiers, log of score plus capped comment points, and the creation time divided by a window: newer stories sort first.

pagecache.title: Inside the page cache refill
pagecache.sub: From refill_story_page_cache in the controller to CachePageJob writing the file.
pagecache.cap: Old stories go on a separate refill_story_pages queue served by one worker, so rebuilding thousands of pages after a deploy never delays a fresh story's refill.

steps.t: Every story write asks for a refill
steps.d: An after_action on create, vote, flag, edit and delete.

steps.t: Already queued in the last 2 minutes?

steps.d: Recent stories on default, older ones on refill_story_pages.
A second job for the same path is discarded.
An in-process HTTPS GET with no session.
Through the patched writer: temp file, then rename.
A retitled story leaves files under its old slug.

comments.title: Inside posting a comment
comments.sub: CommentsController#create, in order. Early exits branch to the right.
comments.cap: Everything slow, telling the people being answered and rebuilding the story page, is queued; the request ends after the save.

steps.d: Text, author and an optional hat.
After commit: first upvote, story counts and hotness, hotspot index.
last_comment_at on the story, last_reply_at on the parent.
A partial for the page's script, or a redirect.

primary.title: Inside the primary database
primary.sub: Six of the tables in db/schema.rb and the two FTS5 indexes. Hover a reference to see the table it points to.
primary.cap: Scores, flags, hotness and comment counts are stored on the rows (denormalised) and recomputed from votes on each change. The FTS5 tables are contentless: they keep only the index, and the models write them in callbacks.

tables.name: stories
tables.note: One submitted link or text post.

fields.note: indexed; the front page orders by it

tables.name: votes
tables.note: Upvotes and flags on stories and comments.

fields.note: what the session cookie points to
typed store: email and Pushover preferences

tables.name: notifications
tables.note: One reply, mention or message for one user.

fields.note: pre-filled when it should not show

tables.name: story_texts
tables.note: Title, description and fetched body of a story, for search.

tables.name: comments_fts · story_texts_fts
tables.note: Contentless FTS5 indexes; rowid is the comment or story id.

entries.t: Design philosophy and the production setup with Hatchbox, step by step.
entries.why: Explains why there is so little infrastructure: the project avoids new services and external dependencies on purpose.

entries.t: Every URL, scoped to explicit formats (html, json, rss).
Which Rails frameworks load, site name and domain, signup switches.
The four SQLite databases: primary, cache, queue, rack_attack.
entries.why: Read this to see that the cache and the queue are databases too; production copies its own file in at deploy.

entries.t: Solid Queue's schedule: page cache prefill, WAL checkpoint, stats, hotspots, backups.
Worker threads and the separate refill_story_pages queue.
Rack::Attack throttles, the page cache patch, SMTP settings, CSP.
Per-IP throttles and their own cache shard.
Atomic, safe file names for the full-page cache.
entries.why: Fixes zero-byte files being served mid-write and path tricks that could overwrite another page's cache file.

entries.t: One controller per area; mod/ holds the moderator tools.
Cookie clearing, the CACHE_PAGE rule and refill_story_page_cache.
All the story lists and their feeds.
Submit, edit, vote, flag, hide and save stories.
Post, edit, vote and list comments.
Flag dashboards, hotspots, bans, merges, mod mail.
Story, Comment, Vote and the rest; most of the rules live here.
entries.why: Story and Comment are large because ranking, validation and callbacks live with the data, so every entry point shares them.

entries.t: Visibility scopes, validations, hotness and URL fetching.
The method that site votes, flags and a story's first upvote go through; a new comment's own upvote is created directly in Comment#record_initial_upvote.
Turns a parsed query into FTS5 matches.
Every background job, run by Solid Queue.
Renders one path and writes it to the page cache.
Reply and mention notifications.
Turns an emailed reply into a comment.
Plain Ruby clients: Sponge (safe HTTP), Mastodon, Pushover, GitHub, Markdown.
entries.why: Outside services are wrapped in a few dozen lines each instead of adding gems, as the README asks.

entries.t: HTTP fetcher that resolves DNS itself and refuses private networks.
The primary database's tables and FTS5 indexes.
Migrations since the move to SQLite; older ones are in db/old_migrations/.
Cron entry points and the mail ingress.
Every 5 minutes: post to Mastodon.
Postfix pipes inbound mail here; it relays to Action Mailbox.
Production server config: Caddy, Anubis, Postfix, systemd, backups.
TLS redirect, bot blocks, and the rules that serve cached pages.
entries.why: The single most important file for performance: it decides when Rails is skipped.

entries.t: Clears the page cache, queues RefillStoryPageCacheJob, moves Puma to 9001.
Development: the web server and bin/jobs side by side.
